scenes.title: Work

beats.text: Syllabus four point five: work done by a force. What work means in mechanics, and how to calculate it.
By the end, you can calculate work as force times distance moved along the force.
beats.caption: Work = force × distance along the force.

beats.text: Use only the part of the force along the motion. The perpendicular part does no work.

scenes.title: Watch the whole journey first

beats.text: Consider a worker dragging a crate up a rough ramp. The rope runs along the ramp, and the crate climbs at a steady speed.
As it climbs, friction drags backwards along the ramp... and the weight pulls straight down. The rope has to beat both.
By the top, the crate has moved a long way along the ramp. But it has only risen a little... a smaller vertical height.
How much work did the rope do against friction? And how much against gravity? Two separate answers.

scenes.title: Work means force times distance moved

beats.text: Push a box along a floor. A force acts, and the box moves along the line of that force. That is mechanical work.
Work done equals force times distance moved along the force.
Newtons times metres. One newton metre is one joule.
Push a wall instead. Nothing moves, so the distance is zero... no work at all, however hard you push.

scenes.title: A force at an angle to the motion

beats.text: Now pull the box with a rope at an angle theta to the floor. The box still moves along the floor.
Only the part of the force along the motion does work: F cos theta.
beats.ink: along the motion: F cos θ

beats.text: So work done equals F d cos theta.
The upward part, F sine theta, is perpendicular to the motion. It moves the box nowhere, so it does no work.
Lift something straight up instead. The force is its weight, m g, and the distance is the height h. Work against gravity is m g h.

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: The full question. A crate of mass four kilograms is dragged five metres up a rough ramp at thirty degrees to the horizontal. Take g as ten.
The rope is parallel to the ramp, and the crate moves at constant speed. The coefficient of friction is zero point two five.
Find the work done against friction, and the work done against gravity.
Before we start: which distance goes with gravity, the five metres along the ramp, or the height? Take a moment.

scenes.title: Work against friction

beats.text: Perpendicular to the ramp, nothing moves, and the rope pulls along the ramp, not away from it. Draw the weight against the ramp.
The part into the ramp is m g cos theta. So the reaction balances it.
R equals forty cos thirty: twenty root three, about thirty-four point six newtons.
The crate is moving, so friction is at its limit: f equals mu R.
Zero point two five times thirty-four point six... about eight point six six newtons, down the ramp.
Work against friction is friction times the distance moved along the ramp.
Eight point six six times five: about forty-three point three joules.

scenes.title: Work against gravity

beats.text: Gravity only cares about height. The crate moves five metres along the ramp, but rises h equals d sine theta.
Five sine thirty is two point five metres. Not five.
Work against gravity is m g h.
Four times ten times two point five: one hundred joules.
More than the friction work here. And notice: constant speed did not mean no work. The rope did both of these.

scenes.title: What would change on a smooth ramp?

beats.text: What if the ramp were smooth? No friction, so no work against friction at all. The work against gravity is unchanged: still one hundred joules, because the height is the same.
